subtitle: Hybrid work can quietly favor whoever is in the room. Learn to reduce proximity bias, run hybrid meetings where location does not decide who is heard, build accessible digital work and tell general telework apart from telework as an accommodation.
audience: For supervisors, team leads, HR partners and staff who plan meetings or assign work on hybrid and remote teams at DHS and DSD. It does not replace the ADA coordinator, HR or labor relations.

lessons.title: Proximity bias and fair visibility
objectives: Explain proximity bias and the research on passive face time.
Summarize what a large randomized trial found about hybrid work, performance and promotion, and its limits.
Identify signals that visibility, not results, is shaping assignments or evaluations.
Plan a consistent review of assignments and recognition using job-related evidence.
lessons.teaching:
Proximity bias is the tendency to favor people you see in person more often. Researchers Kimberly Elsbach, Dan Cable and Jeffrey Sherman studied what they called passive face time: simply being seen at work, without any interaction. In interviews and an experiment, they found that being seen during normal hours led observers to describe someone as dependable, and being seen outside normal hours led observers to describe them as committed. Observers formed these impressions spontaneously, without being aware of it. Being seen was standing in for evidence about work.

That matters in a hybrid workplace, where some people are in the office on a given day and others are not. A supervisor who works on-site may simply know more about the work of people nearby, notice their effort more and think of them first for new assignments. Over time, that can shape who gets visible projects, who is described as a leader and whose name comes up in succession discussions.

Does hybrid work itself hurt performance or advancement? One of the largest studies so far, a randomized trial at a large travel company in China published in the journal Nature, assigned more than sixteen hundred employees to either full-time office work or a hybrid schedule with two home days a week. Hybrid work reduced quitting by about a third, and the researchers found no evidence of differences in performance reviews or promotions over the following two years. Managers who expected hybrid work to lower productivity became more positive after the trial. This is one company in one country with one hybrid design, so it does not settle every question for a Minnesota state agency. It does suggest that remote days do not automatically mean weaker work, but it does not establish how Minnesota agency teams will perform.

Use job-related evidence when making assignments and evaluating performance. Define expected results, essential duties and collaboration requirements, including any necessary on-site work, and apply those criteria consistently. Review authorized assignment and recognition records for patterns that warrant closer examination. Location alone does not establish merit or bias, and equal representation is not a hiring or assignment quota. Before you nominate someone, ask: am I choosing based on results, or on who I happened to see this week?
lessons.keyPoint: Evaluate assignments and recognition against relevant results and job requirements, including necessary on-site duties. Examine whether proximity is influencing the evidence you consider.
lessons.example: Practice case: Benedikta supervises a hybrid DSD team. Three staff work on-site most days because of where they live, and four telework the maximum allowed. When a request comes from the division director for someone to lead a new cross-agency workgroup, Benedikta immediately thinks of Casimir, who sits near her office and often stops by. Afterward, she realizes that Winifred, who teleworks, produced the team's strongest analysis last quarter.
lessons.question: What should Benedikta do before deciding?
choices: Check the workgroup's requirements against recent results from everyone on the team, talk with interested staff and choose on that basis.
Choose Casimir, since in-person availability will matter for a cross-agency workgroup.
Choose Winifred to make up for past favoritism toward on-site staff.
feedback: This is the best response. Benedikta recognizes that her first thought came from proximity and returns to job-related evidence and interest.
Check whether this workgroup actually requires in-person availability. Assuming that proximity makes Casimir better qualified skips the requirements and evidence that Benedikta needs to compare.
Correcting for bias by choosing someone to compensate is still a decision not based on the work. Winifred may be the best choice, but for the right reasons.
lessons.reflection: Whose work do you know best on your team or in your partner network? How much of that knowledge comes from seeing them, and how much from their results?
lessons.action: Using records you are authorized to access, review recent assignments and recognition against the work requirements. Consider whether location affected opportunities; protect personnel information and investigate patterns before drawing conclusions.

check.question: What did Elsbach and colleagues find about passive face time?
check.correct: Being seen at work led observers to infer traits like dependability and commitment, often without realizing it.
wrong: Being seen at work had no effect on how others judged employees.
Observers carefully compared actual output before judging dependability.
check.feedback: The studies found spontaneous trait judgments from being seen. Compare relevant work evidence and requirements rather than treating visibility as proof of dependability or commitment.

lessons.title: Meeting equity in hybrid work
objectives: Identify common ways hybrid meetings disadvantage remote participants.
Plan a meeting structure that gives remote and in-room participants equal access to the conversation and decisions.
Describe accessible meeting practices, including captions and advance materials.
Compare meeting norms and choose ones that fit a specific DHS meeting.
lessons.teaching:
Hybrid meetings can quietly create two classes of participant. People in the room see each other's faces, catch side comments and can jump into a pause. People joining remotely may hear a muffled microphone, see a wide shot of a table, miss what was written on a whiteboard and wait for a gap that never comes. After the meeting, the in-room group may keep talking in the hallway, and decisions get made there. These barriers can arise from the meeting setup even when participants intend to include everyone.

Start with equal access to the conversation. One option is to use separate approved devices, provided participants have usable equipment, bandwidth and privacy. Configure headsets or a single room audio connection to avoid feedback. Do not assume that everyone can use a camera or the same hand-raise control; provide another way to contribute. If a room system is used, test audio before the meeting and make sure remote people can see who is speaking. Name a facilitator who watches the chat and the virtual hands, and invite remote participants to speak first on key questions rather than last.

Next, make information equally available. Send materials ahead of time in accessible formats, so people using screen readers, people with slower connections and people who process better in writing can prepare. Provide captions and check whether their accuracy meets participants’ needs. Automatic captions do not replace an agreed interpreter or communication access service. Share accessible files as well as the screen; a screen image alone may not be usable with assistive technology. Say decisions out loud and write them in the chat or notes, and send a short summary with owners and deadlines. If discussion continues afterward, share the resulting decisions with everyone who needs them. Do not delay urgent authorized action while waiting for another meeting.

Finally, consider the purpose and the people. Choose the format with participants and the meeting’s purpose in mind. Ordinary meeting arrangements do not replace formal Tribal consultation or other required procedures. Address known access barriers promptly, and involve the ADA coordinator or HR when individual accommodation is needed. The question to ask for any meeting is simple: could someone joining from anywhere participate fully, contribute to the decision and know what was decided?
lessons.keyPoint: Provide usable audio, accessible materials, communication access and ways to contribute. Document decisions and choose a meeting format that works for its participants and purpose.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD policy team holds weekly hybrid meetings. Five people sit around a conference table with one camera and one microphone, and four join online. Remote staff often say afterward that they could not hear parts of the discussion. Last week, a remote analyst, Isadora, learned that a key decision about a provider notice had been finalized in a hallway conversation after the meeting. The team lead, Magnus, wants to fix this without adding more meetings. Approved devices, headsets and private connections are available to everyone, and no urgent action depends on the hallway decision.
lessons.question: What change would help most?
choices: Ask remote staff to come into the office on meeting days.
Remind remote staff to speak up more when they cannot hear.

Have everyone join from their own device, use a facilitator to call on remote participants first, turn on captions, and post decisions in writing, including any made after the meeting, before acting on them.
feedback: Requiring attendance shifts the burden to remote staff and may conflict with approved telework or accommodation arrangements. It does not fix the meeting design.
Asking the less-heard group to push harder puts the burden on them. The problem is the setup, not their effort.
This is the best response. It addresses audio, participation order, access and decision transparency together, and it needs no extra meetings.
lessons.reflection: In the last hybrid meeting you attended, who spoke most and who spoke least? How much of that had to do with where people were sitting?
lessons.action: Choose one recurring hybrid meeting you lead or attend. Propose two changes, such as captions on and decisions posted in writing, and ask participants after two weeks whether it helped.

check.question: Why is asking remote participants to speak up more not an effective fix for hybrid meeting inequity?
check.correct: It puts the burden on the people disadvantaged by the meeting design instead of changing the design.
wrong: Because remote participants are not allowed to speak in state meetings.
Because remote staff usually have less to contribute.
check.feedback: The disadvantages come from audio, visibility, turn-taking and decisions made outside the meeting. Changing those conditions works better than asking the people affected to compensate.

lessons.title: Accessible tools and digital accessibility
objectives: Describe the State of Minnesota Digital Accessibility Standard and what it requires.
Distinguish building accessibility into shared tools from handling individual accommodation requests.
Identify common accessibility barriers in remote collaboration tools and documents.
Plan an accessibility check for a document or meeting your team produces.
lessons.teaching:
Remote and hybrid work run on digital tools: video meetings, chat, shared documents, online forms, whiteboards and case management systems. When those tools are not accessible, some employees are shut out of work they are fully able to do, and some people DHS serves are shut out of services. Accessible tools are part of making work and services available to everyone who needs them.

Minnesota’s Digital Accessibility Standard, version 4.0, took effect July 1, 2024. It incorporates qualified Section 508 requirements and WCAG 2.1 levels A and AA, with specified applicability, exceptions and exemptions. Agency staff must apply the applicable standard when creating, changing or procuring technology and content. Ask accessibility staff which requirements apply to an existing system; an exception requires the proper process and does not erase accommodation duties.

It helps to separate two things. Building accessibility in means making shared tools and documents usable by as many people as possible from the start: headings and alt text in documents, readable slides, captions in meetings, color that is not the only way information is conveyed, forms that work with a keyboard and screen reader, and chat tools that do not rely only on emoji or images to carry meaning. Individual accommodation means providing something specific for one person, such as particular assistive technology, a sign language interpreter or a modified schedule. Accommodations go through the supervisor, HR and the agency ADA coordinator. Building accessibility in reduces how often people need to ask, but it does not replace the accommodation process.

Common barriers in remote work are predictable. Whiteboard tools may not work with screen readers. Scanned documents are often images with no readable text. Missing or inaccurate captions can prevent participation; some participants need interpreters or other communication access services. Rapid, overlapping chat can be hard to follow for people using assistive technology. Use built-in accessibility checkers, then review the document or tool manually. Check meaningful headings, reading order, image descriptions, keyboard operation and caption accuracy as relevant. Automated tools cannot establish accessibility, and colleagues with disabilities should not carry sole responsibility for testing. For questions about specific tools, contact your agency's accessibility or MNIT resources.
lessons.keyPoint: Apply Minnesota’s digital accessibility requirements with agency accessibility staff. Address shared barriers promptly and arrange individual accommodations when needed.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team starts using a new online whiteboard for brainstorming in hybrid planning sessions. Most of the team likes it. Leocadia, a team member who uses a screen reader, finds she cannot read or add to the whiteboard and has been emailing her ideas to a colleague to post for her. She has not made a formal request. Her team lead, Rafferty, notices her ideas always arrive late in the discussion.
lessons.question: What is the most appropriate response for Rafferty?
choices: Check with Leocadia privately about what is and is not working, bring the tool's accessibility to MNIT or agency accessibility staff, use an accessible alternative for now, and make sure Leocadia knows how to request an accommodation if she wants one.
Keep using the whiteboard, since Leocadia has found a workaround.
Ask Leocadia to submit an accommodation request so the team can keep using the tool.
feedback: This response addresses immediate exclusion and brings the shared tool to accessibility specialists. A request for disability-related help need not use a formal label; involve HR or the ADA coordinator when needed without waiting to remove a known barrier.
A workaround that depends on a colleague delays her contributions and keeps her out of the live discussion. The tool itself is the barrier.
An accommodation process is available, but the underlying problem is that a shared tool does not meet accessibility expectations. Putting the burden on Leocadia alone misses that.
lessons.reflection: Which tools or document habits on your team might be hard to use for someone with a different way of seeing, hearing, moving or processing information? How would you find out?
lessons.action: Check a document or slide deck with its built-in accessibility tool, then review headings, reading order and meaningful image descriptions manually. Ask accessibility staff about unresolved barriers and confirm communication access for the next meeting.

check.question: What is the difference between building accessibility in and providing an individual accommodation?
check.correct: Building accessibility in makes shared tools usable by many people from the start, while an accommodation is a specific adjustment for one person arranged through the accommodation process.
wrong: They are the same thing under different names.
Building accessibility in is only required when an employee asks for it.
check.feedback: State standards expect digital work to be accessible from the start. Accommodations still exist for specific individual needs. Both matter, and doing the first well reduces how often people have to ask for the second.

lessons.title: Telework as policy and telework as accommodation
objectives: Describe the main features of the statewide telework policy for executive branch employees.
Explain how telework as a reasonable accommodation differs from telework under general policy.
Identify the supervisor's role when an employee asks for more telework for a disability-related reason.
Apply telework policy consistently across team members.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota’s statewide telework rules can change, so check the current policy before approving a schedule. Policy 1422, revised June 1, 2025, allows covered staff with satisfactory performance to work remotely for up to 50% of scheduled workdays each month when business needs allow. Staff who live more than 50 miles from their main work location may receive approval for more remote days. That choice rests with the appointing authority; distance alone does not guarantee approval. The policy excludes mobile workers, remote workers as it defines them, and work at home approved for a particular situation. Staff and supervisors document the agreed schedule and follow agency requirements.

Telework for a disability-related need follows a separate process. EEOC guidance explains that working at home may be a reasonable accommodation even when an employer has no general telework program. The employer may need to change its usual rules, but it may choose another effective option and does not have to remove essential duties. The decision considers the person’s needs, the work and whether an option would cause undue hardship. JAN guidance explains that the schedule should fit the disability-related need, which may require full-time or part-time telework. State policy allows an ADA accommodation acknowledgment to modify its provisions, and MMB identifies several contacts who can receive a request.

A supervisor should recognize a request and connect the employee promptly with HR or the ADA coordinator. An employee need not use a legal term: explaining that a medical condition requires a change in work can begin the process. Do not treat the usual telework limit as a final answer. Participate in the discussion and arrange interim steps within your authority when needed. Leave requests for necessary medical documentation to the authorized process, and do not seek unrelated health details. Keep medical information separate from ordinary personnel records and share it only as permitted for legitimate responsibilities.

Apply ordinary telework rules consistently using work needs and relevant evidence. Being more visible or personally familiar to a supervisor should not decide whose request succeeds. When someone has an accommodation, do not tell colleagues the medical reason. Fair treatment requires consistent general decisions and a separate, responsive process for individual disability-related needs.
lessons.keyPoint: General telework is discretionary under statewide policy. Disability-related telework is an accommodation question that goes to the ADA coordinator or HR through the interactive process, and can go beyond policy limits.
lessons.example: Practice case: Tobiah, a DSD policy analyst, tells his supervisor, Genevieve, that commuting four days a week has become very difficult because of a chronic condition and asks whether he can telework more than the statewide limit. Genevieve wants to help but worries that approving it would be unfair to others who have also asked for more telework. She is tempted to say the limit applies to everyone.
lessons.question: What should Genevieve do?
choices: Tell Tobiah the limit applies to everyone, to keep things fair for the team.
Recognize this as a possible accommodation request, connect Tobiah with the ADA coordinator or HR, take part in the interactive process and keep his health information confidential.
Approve extra telework informally herself, without involving HR, to spare Tobiah paperwork.
feedback: Treating the policy limit as final can deny a reasonable accommodation. The EEOC explains that telework policies may need to be modified for an employee with a disability.

This response connects Tobiah with the people responsible for accommodation decisions and protects his medical information. The interactive process considers essential functions, effectiveness and undue hardship; it may result in telework or another effective accommodation.
Informal approval skips the process that protects Tobiah and the agency, leaves the arrangement undocumented and may be inconsistent with policy. Accommodations need the proper route.
lessons.reflection: If someone on your team asked you for a change in where or when they work, what words would signal that it might be an accommodation request? What would you do first?
lessons.action: Find your agency's ADA coordinator contact and the current statewide telework policy and guidance. If you supervise, check that you apply the general policy the same way to everyone on your team.

check.question: According to the EEOC, can telework be a reasonable accommodation when an employer does not allow other employees to telework?
check.correct: Yes. Changing the location of work can be a reasonable accommodation even when the employer does not generally allow telework, though the employer may choose another effective accommodation.
wrong: No. Accommodations may never go beyond what a general policy allows.
Yes, and the employer must always grant exactly the telework schedule the employee requests.
check.feedback: The ADA can require modifying workplace policies, including telework rules. The employer may still choose among effective accommodations and does not have to remove essential job functions. The interactive process decides what works.

cards.back: Favoring people because they are seen in person more often, rather than comparing relevant evidence and job requirements.
Being seen at work without interacting. Research found it leads observers to spontaneously judge people as dependable or committed.
Minnesota’s standard includes qualified Section 508 requirements and WCAG 2.1 levels A and AA. Apply its scope and exception process with agency accessibility staff.
A staffing arrangement at the appointing authority's discretion under the statewide telework policy, with limits on how many days may be teleworked.
Telework provided as a reasonable accommodation for a disability through the interactive process. It can go beyond general policy limits, and the employer may choose another effective option.

aid.heading: Fair visibility checklist
items: Define expected results for each role and review them the same way for everyone.
Review assignment and recognition records only within your authorized access.
Investigate location-related patterns against actual job requirements; representation alone does not prove bias.
Before nominating someone, ask whether results or presence drove the choice.

aid.heading: Hybrid meeting setup
items: Test an accessible room setup or approved individual devices, with audio configured to prevent feedback.
Name a facilitator to watch chat and raised hands.
Invite remote participants to speak first on key questions.
Send accessible files in advance and confirm captions or other required communication access.
Write decisions down and share any decisions made after the meeting.

aid.heading: When telework or tool access comes up
items: Apply the general telework policy consistently to everyone.
Treat a disability-related request as a possible accommodation even without those words.
Involve the ADA coordinator or HR promptly; use the authorized process for any necessary medical documentation.
Report inaccessible shared tools to agency accessibility or MNIT resources.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1422, Telework (revised 2025)
sources.note: Supports that telework is a discretionary arrangement, the monthly limit on telework days for most employees, the acknowledgment form and that an ADA accommodation acknowledgment can modify the policy. Policy changes, so check the current version.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Memo 2025-1, Telework Frequently Asked Questions
sources.note: Supports that employees may request telework beyond the policy limit as a reasonable accommodation through supervisors, HR or the ADA coordinator, and details on scheduling.

sources.title: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Work at Home/Telework as a Reasonable Accommodation
sources.note: Supports that telework may be a reasonable accommodation even where the employer does not otherwise allow it, that the employer may choose among effective accommodations and need not remove essential functions.

sources.title: Job Accommodation Network — Telework
sources.note: Supports that telework as an accommodation should match what the disability requires and that the employer may choose any effective accommodation. JAN provides guidance, not legal determinations.

sources.title: Bloom, Han and Liang — Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance, Nature (2024)
sources.note: Supports the randomized trial findings on retention, performance reviews, promotions and manager perceptions. The study covers one company in China and may not generalize.

sources.title: Elsbach, Cable and Sherman — How passive face time affects perceptions of employees, Human Relations (2010), UC eScholarship
sources.note: Supports the finding that being seen at work leads observers to spontaneously judge employees as dependable or committed. Based on interviews and an experiment with office workers.

sources.title: Minnesota IT Services — Accessibility Policies and Standards
sources.note: Explains statewide accessibility requirements and links to the current standard and implementation guidance.

sources.title: Minnesota IT Services — State of Minnesota Digital Accessibility Standard, version 4.0
sources.note: Effective July 1, 2024; Section 508 qualifications, WCAG 2.1 A and AA, applicability and documented exceptions.

sources.title: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative — Selecting Web Accessibility Evaluation Tools
sources.note: Automated evaluation cannot determine accessibility by itself; human judgment and manual checks are necessary.

sources.title: Minnesota IT Services — Accessible Meetings
sources.note: Plan communication access, provide accessible materials, test the actual meeting setup, and arrange requested CART rather than substituting automatic captions.
